PORTIA: … Lorenzo, I commit into your hands
The husbandry and manage of my house
Until my lord's return: for mine own part,
I have toward heaven breathed a secret vow
To live in prayer and contemplation,
Only attended by Nerissa here,
Until her husband and my lord's return:
extract.speaker: Portia
extract.context_before: Before leaving Belmont to help save Antonio, Portia entrusts the care of her house to Lorenzo, who has recently married Jessica.

questions.question_text: Who does Portia refer to as 'my lord'? Where is her lord? Why had he left in such haste?
key_points: Bassanio/lover/husband/partner
Gone to Venice/to attend Antonio's trial/court of justice.

Antonio had in a letter asked Bassanio to come and see him one last time before his death/Portia urges him to marry her and leave immediately for Venice/to save Antonio/Bassanio felt responsible for Antonio's condition/Antonio's life was in danger … Shylock demanded a pound of flesh.
questions.scheme_text:
Bassanio/lover/husband/partner
Gone to Venice/to attend Antonio's trial/court of justice.
Antonio had in a letter asked Bassanio to come and see him one last time before his death/Portia urges him to marry her and leave immediately for Venice/to save Antonio/Bassanio felt responsible for Antonio's condition/Antonio's life was in danger … Shylock demanded a pound of flesh.
questions.examiner_comment: Most candidates answered all parts of the question correctly. In the second part, instead of 'Venice', some of them wrote 'Venus'. Many candidates answered that her lord was in Belmont.
questions.teacher_suggestion: The action in the play alternates between Venice and Belmont. Train students to be aware of the setting in each scene.

extract.text:
PORTIA: … Lorenzo, I commit into your hands
The husbandry and manage of my house
Until my lord's return: for mine own part,
I have toward heaven breathed a secret vow
To live in prayer and contemplation,
Only attended by Nerissa here,
Until her husband and my lord's return:
extract.speaker: Portia
extract.context_before: Before leaving Belmont to help save Antonio, Portia entrusts the care of her house to Lorenzo, who has recently married Jessica.

questions.question_text: What do we learn of Portia's real intention from her conversation with Nerissa? Which Portia do you prefer - the modest Portia of the Casket scene or the business-like Portia we meet in this scene? Give one reason for your response.
key_points: Portia plans they would disguise themselves as young men – herself as a lawyer and Nerissa as a lawyer's clerk
travel to Venice/to assist at Antonio's trial
meet with their husbands – (who would not be able to recognise the young ladies as they would be in disguise)
Accept either response 'modest Portia' (humble/generous/gracious/virtuous/demure – accept examples/quotes from the casket scene to show she is modest/humble)
Business-like Portia (strong, independent, smart, empowered, fearless, determined, quick thinking)

real_intention.instruction: State what we learn of Portia's real intention from her conversation with Nerissa.

preference_with_reason.instruction: State which Portia (modest or business-like) is preferred, and give one plausible reason/justification.

questions.scheme_text:
Portia plans they would disguise themselves as young men – herself as a lawyer and Nerissa as a lawyer's clerk
travel to Venice/to assist at Antonio's trial.
meet with their husbands – (who would not be able to recognise the young ladies as they would be in disguise). (Any two)
Accept a plausible justification for either
Accept either response 'modest Portia' (humble/generous/gracious/virtuous/demure – accept examples/quotes from the casket scene to show she is modest/humble)
Business-like Portia (strong, independent, smart, empowered, fearless, determined, quick thinking)
questions.examiner_comment: This question was answered correctly by most of the candidates. It was interesting to note that most of them stated that they preferred the 'business-like Portia' to the 'modest Portia'. Justification for this preference ranged from 'Portia is a strong woman', 'independent person', 'has a mind of her own, capable of independent thinking' to 'she dared to break gender stereotypes'. A few candidates chose both options ('business-like Portia' and 'modest Portia') but were unable to justify their choice. Most candidates provided an accurate description of Portia's real intention.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Discuss reason-based questions in the classroom. This will develop the ability to answer such questions in examinations with honesty and confidence. Create opportunities in the classroom for students to speak their minds, explore characters, and express their opinions.

extract.text:
SHYLOCK: Shall I not have barely my principal?
PORTIA: Thou shalt have nothing but the forfeiture,
To be so taken at thy peril, Jew.
extract.speaker: Shylock and Portia
extract.context_before: During the trial scene, having been denied his money, Shylock insists on taking his bond, and Portia warns him of the strict letter of the law.

questions.question_text: What is the 'principal' that Shylock asks for? Why does Portia refuse to give it to him?
key_points: The three thousand ducats/sum/amount he had loaned to Bassanio.
Shylock (had been offered the sum/larger sums repeatedly in court and) he had refused the offer in open court.
Shylock had stubbornly demanded his bond/the forfeiture/Shylock said he wanted only justice.
questions.scheme_text:
The three thousand ducats/sum/amount he had loaned to Bassanio.
Shylock (had been offered the sum/larger sums repeatedly in court and) he had refused the offer in open court.
Shylock had stubbornly demanded his bond/the forfeiture/Shylock said he wanted only justice. (Any two)
questions.examiner_comment: Most candidates answered all parts of the question correctly and earned marks. Surprisingly many candidates didn't mention the 3000 ducats specifically. Some even confused the '3000 ducats' with the 'pound of flesh'. A number of candidates were unable to answer the second part of the question. Many gave the reason that Portia wanted to save Antonio. Quite a few candidates gave only one reason for Portia's refusal to give Shylock the principal amount.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Ask 'why' questions in the classroom to encourage students to explore and discuss alternative reasons for any given character's action. This will help them to think out of the box.

questions.question_text: Why is Shylock in a hurry to leave the courtroom after the trial? How far can Shylock be blamed for the outcome of the trial? Give one reason for your response.
key_points: Shylock feels shamed and humiliated / he has lost face / defeated / he feels physically ill/ devastated/ angry/ frustrated/ shattered/ sad/ not happy/ disappointed.
Yes, he was largely to blame – stubbornly refused offers of money / refused to be merciful/ insisted on his bond/ tried to kill/ vindictive
OR No, he was shamed and humiliated / reacted in anger and desire for revenge / his was a human response.

questions.scheme_text:
Shylock feels shamed and humiliated / he has lost face / defeated / he feels physically ill/ devastated/ angry/ frustrated/ shattered/ sad/ not happy/ disappointed.
Yes, he was largely to blame – stubbornly refused offers of money / refused to be merciful/ insisted on his bond/ tried to kill/ vindictive
OR
No, he was shamed and humiliated / reacted in anger and desire for revenge / his was a human response.
questions.examiner_comment: Most candidates answered the question correctly. References to Shylock's guilt, shaming, humiliation were made. An inability to express their thoughts due to a lack of adequate vocabulary was observed in the candidates' response to this question. Few candidates could describe Shylock's feelings as devastated/frustrated/shattered/disappointed/humiliated. They simply stated that Shylock was unable to take revenge. The second part of the question was answered well with a proper reason. Most candidates felt that Shylock was to be blamed for the outcome of the trial. A few felt he was the victim and not the villain.

extract.text: "What is to be done with the children?" That was the chief question now. The dead mother would go underground, and be forever beyond all care or concern of the villagers. But the children must not be left to starve.
extract.context_before: The story opens after the death of a poor, drunken woman, leaving the villagers of the town to decide what will become of her three children.

questions.question_text: Describe the way in which the children's mother died. What are the factors that led to her death?
key_points: Fell on the threshold of her house/in a drunken fit (in the presence of her children)
Idleness / vice / intemperance

how_she_died.instruction: Describe the way in which the mother died.

factors.instruction: State the factors that led to her death.

questions.scheme_text:
Fell on the threshold of her house/ in a drunken fit (in the presence of her children)
Idleness / vice / intemperance (Any two)
questions.examiner_comment: The candidates could not distinguish between the two parts of the question. Candidates failed to describe the manner ('how') in which the mother had died. Instead, they listed the causes ('why') for her death. Most candidates named drinking as a factor. Only a few mentioned 'vice' and 'idleness'. They only wrote the mother died due to the excessive consumption of alcohol. They were not able to mention the factors that led to the death of the mother. Many candidates mentioned 'gate/edge/house door/front gate/stairs' instead of 'threshold'. Many candidates could not attempt the second sub-part correctly. They wrote only one factor that led to the lady's death while the question mentioned 'factors' - implying that they were required to list more than one.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Help students in distinguishing between 'HOW' and 'WHY'. Teach students to respond to each sub-question separately.

extract.text: "What is to be done with the children?" That was the chief question now. The dead mother would go underground, and be forever beyond all care or concern of the villagers. But the children must not be left to starve.
extract.context_before: The story opens after the death of a poor, drunken woman, leaving the villagers of the town to decide what will become of her three children.

questions.question_text: How do the people of the village treat the woman before her death? How does their manner change after she dies? What does their behaviour tell us about human nature?
key_points: They scoffed at her/despised/denounced her while she was alive/looked down on her/treated her badly.
Pity / sorrow (replaced their anger and denunciation)
Death touches the spring of our common humanity/people are compassionate in the face of death/forgive and forget/fickleness of humans/fleeting sentiments.
questions.scheme_text:
They scoffed at her /despised / denounced her while she was alive/ looked down on her/ treated her badly.
Pity / sorrow (replaced their anger and denunciation)
Death touches the spring of our common humanity/ people are compassionate in the face of death/ forgive and forget/ fickleness of humans / fleeting sentiments.
questions.examiner_comment: Most candidates were able to describe 'how the villagers treated the mother before/after her death'. However, many were unable to say why ['what this tells us of human nature…?'] there was a change in their manner after her death i.e., the candidates were unable/afraid to draw an inference/afraid to express an opinion. The first two parts of the question were answered well, but many candidates did not fully comprehend the words, 'death touches the spring of humanity' or 'people are compassionate in the face of death'. It was noticed that the candidate often did not know how to answer the sub questions specifically. Instead, they wrote responses that were a page long and the examiners had to wade through that to find the answers.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Encourage more discussion in class – create opportunities in the classroom for students to express their views and challenge/debate opinions that are different from their own.

extract.context_before: The story opens after the death of a poor, drunken woman, leaving the villagers of the town to decide what will become of her three children.

questions.question_text: Name the woman's three children. State one fact about each of them that the author mentions at the very beginning of the story.
key_points: John + Kate + Maggie
Description of ANY TWO children/ One child with full, correct description
John + oldest – boy of twelve – stout lad – able to earn his living with any farmer.
Kate – between ten and eleven – bright active girl – if in good hands she would blossom into a clever person.
Maggie – youngest – hopelessly diseased / injured spine after a fall from a window.

facts.instruction: State one fact about each of any two children (or one child with full, correct description) that the author mentions at the beginning of the story.

questions.scheme_text:
John + Kate + Maggie
Description of ANY TWO children/ One child with full, correct description
John + oldest – boy of twelve – stout lad – able to earn his living with any farmer.
Kate – between ten and eleven – bright active girl – if in good hands she would blossom into a clever person.
Maggie – youngest – hopelessly diseased / injured spine after a fall from a window.
questions.examiner_comment: Candidates answered this as one single question. It was easy enough for them to write the names of the three children mentioning at least one fact about each one of them. Some candidates who were unfamiliar with the text struggled to recall the names and often managed only two correct names. Some candidates had trouble with naming the children correctly. Many candidates had trouble spelling the names of the children in the story. E.g., 'John' was spelt as 'Jhon' and 'Ellis' as 'Alis'.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Remembering the names of the characters in a story is a basic requirement. Regular quizzes on factual details often help students remember such details during the examinations. Dictation or Spell-Bee competitions should be held in schools to improve their spelling.

extract.text:
"Margot"
They stood as if someone had driven them like so many stakes into the floor. They looked at each other and then looked away. They glanced out at the world that was raining now and raining and raining steadily. They could not meet each other's glances. Their faces were solemn and pale. They looked at their hands and feet, their faces down.
extract.context_before: On planet Venus, where the sun appears only once every seven years, the other children resent Margot, who remembers Earth's sunshine and cannot stop talking about it.

Physical: frail; pale (washed out blue eyes, pale lips and light coloured hair)/like an old photograph that had lost all its colour/soft, faint voice/like a ghost.
Personality: withdrawn/ kept to herself/ incredibly passionate about the sun/ different from the others/ introvert/ victim of bullying/ alienated

description.instruction: Describe Margot, physical or personality traits.

questions.scheme_text:

Description (any two from either physical/ personality)
Physical: frail; pale (see text: washed out blue eyes, pale lips and light coloured hair) /like an old photograph that had lost all its colour/ soft, faint voice/ like a ghost.
Personality: withdrawn/ kept to herself/ incredibly passionate about the sun/ different from the others/ introvert/ victim of bullying/ alienated
questions.examiner_comment: Candidates unfamiliar with textual detail, found it difficult to describe Margot. Some candidates were unable to say more than, 'a girl/ a little girl' in response to the first part of this question. Most candidates were able to provide a physical description of Margot, but very few mentioned about her personality. Some candidates did not describe her appearances/ personality; they only mentioned that she was a nine-year-old girl living on planet Venus. In the third part of the question, some candidates actually gave a factual description of the planet Venus (as the Earth's neighbouring planet, closer to sun, hotter than the Earth etc.) …! Students were expected to use words like 'withdrawn'/ 'alienated' / 'introvert' /'passionate about the Sun' in their descriptions of Margot.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Encourage students to pay close attention to textual detail – especially descriptive details.

questions.examiner_comment: Most candidates answered both parts of the question correctly. They were familiar with details of Angelou's early years and her struggle as an activist, feminist and a person of colour and made references to all this in their responses. Some candidates mentioned only one difference instead of two in response to the second part of this question. Several candidates mentioned the differences between white Americans and African Americans.
